## Spinning came first

The order matters and students always get it backwards. Spinning was the bottleneck: one weaver needed the yarn of several spinners. So the inventions come in spinning:

- James Hargreaves, spinning jenny, about 1764, patented 1770. Hand-powered, used at home.
- Richard Arkwright, water frame, patented 1769. Needed a river, so it needed a mill.
- Samuel Crompton, the mule, 1779. Combined the two, fine strong yarn. He never patented it and got a £5,000 grant from Parliament in 1812, which he thought an insult.

Arkwright's Cromford Mill on the Derwent opened in 1771 and ran day and night in two 12-hour shifts. That is the moment the factory clock arrives.

## Weaving lagged behind

Edmund Cartwright, a clergyman with no textile background, patented the power loom in 1785. It took decades to work properly. In the meantime, handloom weaving boomed and then collapsed. E. P. Thompson, *The Making of the English Working Class* (Penguin, 1968), p. 297 has the wage series for Bolton weavers: about 25 shillings a week in 1800, down to around 5s 6d by 1830. That collapse is the human centre of the topic for me.

## Quarry Bank, Easter 2024

Visited Styal on 3 April 2024 on the way back from a conference in Manchester. Samuel Greg built the mill in 1784. Ticket £21. The Apprentice House is the part to see: up to 90 pauper children at a time, bound until 18, two to a bed. The guide, a retired Macclesfield teacher called Hilary, ran the weaving shed demonstration for us. Four looms going at once and I measured 88 dB on my phone. With 300 looms the hands lip-read to talk.

Bought the guidebook (£6.50) and a postcard of the 1790 apprentice indenture for the classroom wall.

## The Luddites

1811 to 1816, starting in Nottinghamshire with the stocking frames, then the Yorkshire croppers and the Lancashire weavers. Letters signed "General Ludd" or "King Ludd". The Frame Breaking Act of 1812 made it a capital offence. Byron's maiden speech in the House of Lords, 27 February 1812, was against that bill.

Point I make to fifth years: the Luddites were not against technology as such. They were skilled men objecting to cheap, badly made goods and to the loss of a trade they had served seven years to learn.

## Ireland's version

- Belfast linen. By 1850 the Lagan valley was the biggest linen area in the world. My great-great-grandmother may have been a spinner there (see [[Family tree research]]).
- Malcomson's cotton mill at Portlaw, Co. Waterford, opened 1825. A planned village, about 1,800 hands at its peak.
- Balbriggan stockings, sold as far as the US.
- The Liberties silk weavers in Dublin, ruined by the end of tariff protection after the 1820s.

## The law catches up

Factory Act 1833: no children under 9 in textile mills, under-13s limited to 9 hours, and 4 inspectors for the whole country. Four. Then the Ten Hours Act of 1847.

## Robert Owen

New Lanark, from 1800. Infant school, no children under 10, a shop selling at near cost. I want to see it on the [[Road trip Scotland]] we keep talking about.

## For class

Second years, 4 lessons. Source exercise IR-2Y-02 pairs a Factory Inspector's report with a page of Crompton's own complaint letter. Ask the same question I ask after [[Printing press]]: who gained, who lost, and how fast?
